title: When Walmart Leaves, the Stores Next Door Lose Too

source.author: Vivek Astvansh, Preetinder Kaur, Pushpinder Gill
source.title: When Walmart pulls out of town, the stores next door don't pick up its shoppers: their sales are down 20% a year later
source.checked_against: Single source: a research summary written by the study's own authors. Figures come only from this article; no second report of the study was looked for. The source's 'roughly a quarter' overall figure is not used, because the article also gives a month-by-month path ending at 20% and the two were not reconciled.

figures.text: three authors; article from The Conversation, published by Fortune
figures.quote: Vivek Astvansh, Preetinder Kaur, and Pushpinder Gill

paragraphs: When a Walmart store closes, shoppers often perceive it as bad news. But what happens to the other stores near it? Many people expect them to win, because a big rival is gone. A new study says the opposite is true.

Three researchers wrote about the study for The Conversation, and Fortune shared it. They looked at 39 Walmart stores that closed in 20 states between 2019 and 2026. They used monthly data on how many shoppers visited the stores nearby and how much they spent. Then they compared these stores with similar stores near Walmarts that stayed open.

The results are remarkable. In the first month after a Walmart closed, sales at nearby stores were about 5 percent lower. In the second month, they were about 6 percent lower. After nine months, they were about 17 percent lower. After a year, they were 20 percent lower.

Why does this happen? The researchers describe two forces. The first is good for the neighbors. When a strong opponent disappears, its shoppers need to buy things somewhere else. The second force is bad. A big Walmart is a destination. People come to it, and then they also visit the smaller stores around it. When the Walmart disappears, fewer people have a reason to come to the area. The study shows that the second force can dominate the first. In other words, the bad effect is bigger than the good one.

Nevertheless, not every store lost the same amount. A food store is a close substitute for Walmart, so it can win some of Walmart's old shoppers. A store that sells very different things is not a good substitute, so it wins fewer of them. Stores with famous brands also did better than stores without a known name. And stores that got a bigger share of their money from online orders were less vulnerable. They did not rely on people walking in the door. Stores that sell only in person are more vulnerable.

The study highlights a simple idea. A big store is not only a rival to its neighbors. It also brings people to them. Many small stores are dependent on the big store next door, even if they do not perceive it.

The researchers give advice to three groups. For retailers, the best protection is to have more than one location or to sell more online. For property owners, it is important to find a new business quickly. But it should be a business that brings people to the area. For local governments, the problem is bigger than one empty building. In the worst scenario, a whole shopping area loses its shoppers.

The lesson is distinct from what many people expect. Losing an opponent can hurt. A big store can dominate a whole shopping area. In this scenario, the stores next door are more dependent on Walmart than they think.
